strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: retaining information across long offline-RL trajectories while keeping the transformer context bounded.

The strongest evidence is the T-Maze retention ablation: at corridor length 900, MRV achieves 0.90 ± 0.07 success versus 0.61 ± 0.07 without MRV (Table 6). The ViZDoom improvement over DT is also substantial.

The evaluation covers several observation types and task families. Comparisons between memory-update designs, cue-removal experiments, memory perturbations, and curriculum ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence.
The appendices document dataset construction, hyperparameters, repeated-run counts, and hardware usage, and the manuscript supplies a code link.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is incremental: recurrent memory tokens and hidden-state caching come from RMT and Transformer-XL, while MRV applies standard cross-attention. A stronger distinction from existing memory-update mechanisms is needed. Controlled architectural ablations concentrate on T-Maze and ViZDoom, leaving MRV's contribution on the richer memory tasks insufficiently established.

Important comparisons do not isolate the memory contribution. Appendix D removes feed-forward blocks from RATE while retaining them in the transformer baselines. For MuJoCo, RATE additionally resets the target return at segment boundaries without a corresponding baseline control. Both changes can independently affect performance; matched ablations are necessary to attribute improvements to the proposed memory mechanisms.

The recurrent-baseline results raise unresolved optimization concerns. LSTM, GRU, and Mamba all obtain exactly 50% success on T-Maze even at the training horizon of 90 steps (Table 1). Without architecture-specific training details, tuning, and convergence diagnostics, these failures do not justify the broad claim that RNNs and SSMs cannot handle sparse long-term memory.

The claim of significant superiority across memory-intensive environments exceeds the evidence. Memory Maze reports 7.64 ± 0.41 versus RMT's 7.27 ± 0.21, using SEM over only three runs; a reliable improvement is not established. On Minigrid, RATE trails TrXL on smaller grids and RMT on larger grids. The clearest retention gains therefore remain concentrated in relatively simple cue-recall settings.

The asserted ordering R[OracleDT] ≥ R[RATE] ≥ R[DT] in Section 5 is not guaranteed. Privileged information does not make a particular trained neural policy an upper bound on another policy, and adding memory does not guarantee improved return. OracleDT should be presented as an empirical privileged-information reference.

Technical reporting needs correction. Algorithm 1 does not specify cache updates or gradient propagation and truncation across segments. Appendix G's parameter difference, d_model × num_mem_tokens, omits the trainable MRV projections and does not account for feed-forward removal. Complete training/inference specifications and accurate per-model parameter counts are needed to substantiate reproducibility and efficiency claims.
